clinicalPearls: Urticaria (hives) are well-circumscribed wheals (dilation of superficial dermal vessels) that are intensely pruritic, often migrate, individually last <24 h, and resolve without bruising or scarring; angioedema arises from deeper dermis/subcutaneous tissue with more pain than pruritus and minimal erythema, taking hours to days to resolve (p.2807).

Urticaria and angioedema reflect similar pathophysiology at different skin levels and often co-occur, with roughly 40% of patients reporting both; together they affect >20% of the population at some point in life (p.2807).

Acute urticaria/angioedema are episodes lasting <6 weeks (usually food, environmental, or drug allergen, or viral infection); attacks persisting >6 weeks are termed chronic and are often spontaneous/idiopathic with no identifiable cause. More than two-thirds of new-onset cases are ultimately diagnosed as acute (p.2807).

Inducible (physical) urticarias are identified by the precipitating stimulus: dermatographism (linear wheal after brisk stroke, affects 2-5%), cholinergic urticaria (small 1-2 mm pruritic wheals with large surrounding erythema triggered by a rise in core body temperature such as fever, hot bath, or exercise), cold, solar, pressure, vibratory, heat, aquagenic, and contact urticaria; most inducible-urticaria lesions individually last <2 h (p.2807-2808).

Hereditary angioedema (HAE) is a fully penetrant autosomal dominant disorder from SERPING1 mutation causing C1 inhibitor (C1INH) deficiency (type 1, ~85%) or dysfunctional protein (type 2); presentation in childhood/adolescence and a family history of angioedema are distinguishing features (p.2808).

HAE diagnosis is suggested by family history, early age of onset, lack of pruritus and urticarial lesions, recurrent gastrointestinal colic, episodes of laryngeal edema, and failure to respond to H1 antihistamines; laboratory confirmation shows low C1INH antigen (type 1) or nonfunctional protein (type 2), with chronically depleted C4 and C2 that fall further during attacks (p.2808-2809).

Cold urticaria can be confirmed by ice-cube placement on the volar forearm provoking a wheal within minutes; cryoglobulins or cold agglutinins are present in up to 5% of these patients, and immersion in cold water (swimming) can progress to vascular collapse (p.2807-2808).

Up to 45% of chronic urticaria has an autoimmune basis, including autoantibodies to IgE or to the alpha chain of FcepsilonRI, and may be associated with antithyroid antibodies (antimicrosomal peroxidase/thyroglobulin) in both Hashimoto's thyroiditis and a euthyroid state (p.2808).

Allergic rhinitis is characterized by sneezing, rhinorrhea, nasal obstruction, lacrimation, and itching of the conjunctiva/nasal mucosa/oropharynx; the nasal mucosa is classically pale and boggy. It requires a temporal relationship to allergen exposure plus documented IgE sensitization (p.2808-2809).

Allergic rhinitis usually occurs in atopic individuals and overlaps strongly with other atopic disease: up to 50% of allergic rhinitis patients have asthma, while 70-80% of asthmatics and 80% of those with chronic bilateral sinusitis have allergic rhinitis (p.2809).

Seasonal allergic rhinitis is elicited by wind-pollinated tree, grass, and weed pollens (in temperate North America: trees Mar-May, grasses Jun-early Jul, weeds mid-Aug-early Oct); perennial rhinitis is driven by year-round allergens such as dust mites (Dermatophagoides), animal dander, cockroach proteins, and mold spores (p.2809).
Pollen-associated (oral allergy) food syndrome causes oropharyngeal pruritus and/or mild swelling after ingesting plant foods cross-reactive with the offending tree, grass, or weed pollen (p.2809).
harrison.pathophysiology: Atopy is a tendency to manifest asthma, rhinitis, urticaria, food allergy, and atopic dermatitis in association with allergen-specific IgE, though urticaria and anaphylaxis can also occur in non-atopic individuals. Mast cells are the key effector cells: IgE binds the high-affinity receptor FcepsilonRI (sensitization), and antigen-driven receptor aggregation triggers Lyn/Syk/Fyn tyrosine-kinase signaling, calcium influx, and degranulation. This releases preformed granule mediators (histamine, tryptase, chymase, carboxypeptidase A, proteoglycans), newly generated lipid mediators (PGD2 via cyclooxygenase; LTB4 and cysteinyl leukotrienes LTC4/D4/E4 via 5-lipoxygenase/FLAP; PAF), and cytokines/chemokines (TNF-alpha, IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, GM-CSF). Mast cells can also be activated IgE-independently via C5a/C3a anaphylatoxin receptors, TLRs, alarmin (TSLP, IL-33) receptors, and MRGPRX2 (a target of small-molecule drugs such as ciprofloxacin and rocuronium and of neuropeptides). Histamine and lipid mediators increase venular permeability producing dermal edema (urticaria) or deeper subcutaneous/dermal edema (angioedema). Cold urticaria provides the best evidence for IgE/mast-cell involvement, with documented mast cell degranulation and elevated lesional histamine. In contrast, bradykinin-mediated angioedema (HAE from C1INH deficiency, or ACE inhibitor-induced) results from excess bradykinin: C1INH normally inhibits activated factor XII, kallikrein, and C1r/C1s, and its deficiency leads to bradykinin accumulation with falling C4/C2. Allergic rhinitis arises from sensitized intraepithelial and perivenular nasal mast cells that, on allergen exposure, release histamine, PGD2, and leukotrienes, producing submucosal edema and eosinophilic infiltration.
additionalDifferentials: Acute vs chronic urticaria/angioedema (cutoff 6 weeks duration)
Inducible (physical) urticarias: dermatographism, cholinergic, cold, solar, pressure, vibratory, heat, aquagenic, contact
Urticarial vasculitis (immune-complex disease; small-vessel leukocytoclastic vasculitis)
Hereditary angioedema (C1INH type 1/2; type 3 with normal C1INH e.g. factor XII mutation)
Acquired C1INH deficiency (lymphoproliferative or autoimmune disease)
CIAS1/NLRP3-associated periodic fever syndromes (familial cold autoinflammatory syndrome, Muckle-Wells syndrome)
Schnitzler's syndrome, Gleich's syndrome, hypereosinophilic syndrome
Serum sickness and hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis

Allergic rhinitis: nonallergic rhinitis with eosinophilia (NARES), vasomotor/perennial nonallergic rhinitis, rhinitis medicamentosa, gustatory rhinitis, hormonal (pregnancy) rhinitis, drug-induced rhinitis, hypothyroidism, anatomic/structural nasal defects, nasal foreign body
infectionMimics: Viral infection-associated acute urticaria (a common trigger of new-onset acute urticaria)
Bacterial or parasitic infection-associated urticaria (travel history should prompt parasite evaluation)
Hepatitis B or C and SARS-CoV-2 infection associated with urticaria/urticarial vasculitis
Upper respiratory tract infection mimicking rhinitis; secondary bacterial sinusitis/otitis from mucosal swelling
nonInfectiousMimics: Urticarial vasculitis (lesions >24 h, painful/burning rather than pruritic, residual petechiae/bruising)
Mastocytosis presenting with flushing and hyperpigmented papules that urticate on stroking (Darier's sign)
Vasomotor (nonallergic) rhinitis and NARES mimicking allergic rhinitis
additionalInvestigations: History-directed skin testing (puncture/prick) or serum allergen-specific IgE for suspected allergen triggers
Provocation/threshold testing for inducible urticaria (e.g. ice-cube test for cold urticaria; stroking for dermatographism)
Limited labs in unrevealing chronic urticaria: CBC with eosinophil assessment, ESR or CRP (most chronic urticaria has no lab abnormality)
Skin biopsy for lesions lasting >36 h, scarring, or painful/non-pruritic - to assess for urticarial vasculitis (cellular infiltrate, nuclear debris, fibrinoid venular necrosis)
For isolated angioedema: basic chemistries with liver function tests and complement levels
C1INH antigen level and functional (catalytic inhibition) assay, with C4 and C2 levels, for suspected HAE; C1q and C1 function additionally reduced in acquired C1INH deficiency
Evaluation for paraproteinemia/lymphoproliferative disease where presentation suggests acquired C1INH deficiency
Autologous serum skin test and basophil activation markers (CD63/CD203) for autoimmune chronic urticaria; antithyroid antibodies
Nasal secretion eosinophils and serum/skin specific IgE for allergic rhinitis (skin test more sensitive; serum specific IgE less sensitive but highly specific)
redFlags: Angioedema of the upper respiratory tract / larynx may be life-threatening due to transient laryngeal obstruction - airway emergency
Gastrointestinal angioedema with abdominal colic can mimic an acute abdomen and lead to unnecessary surgical intervention
Cold urticaria with cold-water immersion may progress to vascular collapse
Progression of urticaria/angioedema to anaphylaxis with vascular collapse (e.g. exercise-induced anaphylaxis, food/drug triggers)
Urticarial lesions lasting >24-36 h with bruising/petechiae, scarring, or burning/pain rather than pruritus suggest urticarial vasculitis and warrant biopsy
harrison.prognosis: More than two-thirds of new-onset urticaria cases are ultimately acute and self-limited. Chronic spontaneous urticaria is most common in the third to fifth decades and the vast majority shows no laboratory abnormality. Dermatographism generally has a duration of <5 years. Allergic rhinitis prevalence in North America is 10-30% (peak >30% in the fifth decade). Allergen immunotherapy (SCIT/SLIT) for allergic rhinitis provides durable symptom benefit and can reduce asthma symptoms; guidelines recommend 3-5 years of SCIT with discontinuation after minimal symptoms over two consecutive allergen seasons.
pitfalls: Failing to distinguish histaminergic from bradykinin-mediated angioedema: bradykinin-mediated angioedema (hereditary angioedema from C1INH deficiency, and ACE inhibitor-induced) is conspicuously WITHOUT concomitant urticaria or pruritus, frequently involves the GI tract, lasts >24 h, and characteristically does NOT respond to H1 antihistamines (nor to adrenaline) - treat with C1INH replacement, bradykinin B2-receptor antagonist (icatibant), or kallikrein inhibitor rather than antihistamines.

Mistaking urticarial vasculitis for simple urticaria: individual lesions persist >24 h, may leave bruising/petechiae and scarring, and cause burning rather than pruritus - biopsy shows leukocytoclastic vasculitis and may signal underlying SLE, Sjogren's, or complement deficiency.
Overlooking laryngeal angioedema as an airway emergency, or mistaking GI angioedema for a surgical abdomen.
Topical glucocorticoids are of no value in urticaria, and systemic glucocorticoids are generally avoided in idiopathic, allergen-induced, or inducible urticaria due to long-term toxicity.
Prolonged use of topical alpha-adrenergic nasal decongestants (7-14 days) causes rebound rhinitis medicamentosa.

Concomitant beta-adrenergic blocker therapy increases the risk of severe/refractory anaphylaxis during allergen immunotherapy; immunotherapy is contraindicated in significant cardiovascular disease or unstable asthma.
harrison.severityClassification: Urticaria/angioedema classified by duration: acute = episodes lasting <6 weeks; chronic = attacks persisting >6 weeks (Table 363-1 further classifies by precipitating factor into acute vs chronic categories, including drug, food, infection, physical/inducible, autoimmune, vasculitic, mastocytosis, and hereditary forms). Hereditary angioedema typed as: type 1 (low C1INH antigen, ~85%), type 2 (dysfunctional C1INH protein), and type 3 (normal C1INH/complement, often identifiable gene mutation e.g. factor XII). Allergic rhinitis classified as seasonal vs perennial, and managed by severity (mild vs moderate-to-severe).
management: Identify and avoid triggers, including implicated foods, drugs such as NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors, and the physical stimuli of inducible urticaria
Treat histaminergic urticaria and angioedema first-line with second-generation non-sedating H1 antihistamines, escalating the dose in chronic spontaneous urticaria
Add omalizumab (anti-IgE) or ciclosporin for antihistamine-refractory chronic spontaneous urticaria, using only short courses of oral corticosteroids for severe flares
Treat allergic rhinitis with allergen avoidance, intranasal corticosteroids and antihistamines, and consider allergen immunotherapy for persistent disease
Treat mast-cell-mediated anaphylaxis with intramuscular adrenaline and provide an adrenaline auto-injector with an emergency plan

Manage hereditary angioedema on the distinct bradykinin pathway, which does not respond to antihistamines, corticosteroids or adrenaline: treat acute attacks with C1-inhibitor concentrate or the bradykinin-receptor antagonist icatibant, provide prophylaxis with C1-inhibitor, lanadelumab or attenuated androgens, and avoid ACE inhibitors and oestrogens
Refer to allergy or immunology for confirmed hereditary angioedema, recurrent anaphylaxis, or difficult chronic urticaria
